L7@P1: Steven Adler-Golden and Patrick Conforti
L8@P1: Spectral Sciences, Inc., Burlington, MA 01803
L9@P1: Marc-André Gagnon, Pierre Tremblay and Martin Chamberland
L10@P1: Telops Inc., Québec, Qc, Canada G2E 6J5
L11@P1: ABSTRACT
L12@P1: Processing long-wave infrared (LWIR) hyperspectral
L13@P1: imagery to surface spectral emissivity or reflectance units
L14@P1: via atmospheric compensation and temperature-emissivity
L15@P1: separation (TES) affords the opportunity to remotely classify
L16@P1: and identify surface materials with minimal interference
L17@P1: from atmospheric effects. This paper describes an
L18@P1: automated atmospheric compensation and TES method,
L19@P1: called FLAASH-IR (Fast Line-of-sight Atmospheric
L20@P1: Analysis of Spectral Hypercubes – Infrared), and its
L21@P1: application to airborne imagery taken with the Telops Inc.
L22@P1: Hyper-Cam interferometric hyperspectral imager. The
L23@P1: results demonstrate good suppression of the atmospheric
L24@P1: features due to water vapor and ozone, resulting in
L25@P1: quantitative surface spectra, even with highly reflective (low
L26@P1: emissivity) objects such as bare metal.
L27@P1: Index Terms— hyperspectral, thermal, infrared,
L28@P1: emissivity, atmospheric correction
L29@P1: 1. INTRODUCTION
L30@P1: Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) technology provides a wealth
L31@P1: of information for remotely identifying and characterizing
L32@P1: surface materials and objects based on their spectral
L33@P1: signatures. Long-wave and mid-wave infrared (L/MWIR)
L34@P1: HSI sensors yield both surface emissivity spectra and
L35@P1: temperatures if the atmospheric effects are removed and the
L36@P1: retrieved surface emission is factored into emissivity and
L37@P1: Planck function components. Since precise knowledge of
L38@P1: the atmospheric conditions is not generally available, the
L39@P1: atmospheric description must be retrieved from the image
L40@P1: itself. Removal of the atmospheric components is
L41@P1: commonly called atmospheric compensation or correction,
L42@P1: while the emissivity retrieval is called
L43@P1: temperature/emissivity separation (TES).
L44@P1: Atmospheric compensation methods are less well
L45@P1: established in the L/MWIR than in the visible-shortwave IR
L46@P1: region due to the added complexity introduced by thermal
L47@P1: emission. In addition, atmospheric compensation is formally
L48@P1: an underdetermined problem: the atmospheric properties are
L49@P1: usually imprecisely known, and the emissivity spectrum and
L50@P1: temperature for a given pixel are presumably unknown as
L51@P1: well, so there are more unknowns than available spectral
L52@P1: channels. Atmospheric compensation and TES solutions
L53@P1: have been developed using a variety of constraints on the
L54@P1: spectrum and atmospheric representation as well as a variety
L55@P1: of mathematical methods [1-5].
L56@P1: A straightforward hyperspectral TES approach suitable
L57@P1: for materials with arbitrary emissivity was developed by
L58@P1: Borel [6] based on maximizing emissivity spectral
L59@P1: smoothness, and was later extended to atmospheric retrieval
L60@P1: [7]. In this paper, we describe a related smoothness-based
L61@P1: automated atmospheric compensation and TES method,
L62@P1: called FLAASH-IR (Fast Line-of-sight Atmospheric
L63@P1: Analysis of Spectral Hypercubes – InfraRed), and its
L64@P1: application to imagery taken from an aircraft with the Telops
L65@P1: Inc. Hyper-Cam interferometric hyperspectral imager. A
L66@P1: recent paper [8] describes an application of FLAASH-IR to
L67@P1: ground-to-ground Hyper-Cam imagery.
L68@P1: 2. CALCULATION OVERVIEW
L69@P1: The LWIR spectral radiance measured by a sensor viewing
L70@P1: objects on the ground can be written as
L71@P1: Lobs() = B(T,)()() + [1 - ()]L() + L() (1)
L72@P1: where  is wavelength, () is the composition- and
L73@P1: temperature-averaged spectral emissivity of the surface
L74@P1: pixel, () is the total (diffuse plus direct) transmittance
L75@P1: between the surface and the sensor, B(T,) is the surface
L76@P1: Planck blackbody function at temperature T, L() is the
L77@P1: transmitted incident illumination, and L() is the
L78@P1: atmospheric path radiance. T is effectively an emissivityweighted average within each pixel. Eq. (1) is rigorous for
L79@P1: Lambertian surfaces; for specular surfaces the emissivity and
L80@P1: illumination quantities may be regarded as “effective.” In
L81@P1: FLAASH-IR (), L() and L() are simulated for a given
L82@P1: set of atmospheric properties using the MODTRAN5®
L83@P1-2: model [9]. Hyperspectral channels are typically narrow enough that within-channel variations in emissivity and the
L84@P2: blackbody function can be neglected. Therefore the
L85@P2: atmospheric radiance and transmittance parameters in Eq.
L86@P2: (1) are convolved with the wavelength response functions
L87@P2: and assigned to their center wavelengths.
L88@P2: 2.1. Temperature and Emissivity Separation (TES)
L89@P2: For a given model atmosphere defining the transmittance,
L90@P2: path and illumination radiances, Eq. (1) leads to a family of
L91@P2: emissivity spectrum solutions corresponding to a range of
L92@P2: possible surface temperature:

L100@P2: The quantities in Eq. (2) are implicitly wavelength

L102@P2: the most likely solution is the one with the least spectral fine
L103@P2: structure. A useful measure of emissivity fine structure is
L104@P2: the mean square residual between the emissivity spectrum
L105@P2: and the same spectrum smoothed with a running average
L106@P2: over spectral channels, denoted as <>. A better measure,
L107@P2: adopted in FLAASH-IR, is obtained by inserting <> into
L108@P2: Eq. (1) and taking the mean square of the difference between

L118@P2: this measure is uniformly weighted across all wavelengths,
L119@P2: regardless of atmospheric optical depth, it enables inclusion
L120@P2: of optically thick wavelengths, where emissivity is poorly
L121@P2: determined but there is valuable information on the
L122@P2: atmosphere. The unsmoothed emissivity spectrum from Eq.
L123@P2: (2) is reported as the retrieval result. To reduce sensitivity
L124@P2: to sensor artifacts, such as wavelength or instrument
L125@P2: function miscalibration, we use a fairly wide smoothing
L126@P2: window of around ~0.3-0.5 m (typically ~7-11 channels),
L127@P2: which suppresses coarse as well as fine spectral features.
L128@P2: The TES generally benefits from restricting the analysis
L129@P2: to the ~9-10.2 m region around the ozone band, whose
L130@P2: presence in the surface spectrum directly correlates with
L131@P2: reflectance (1-emissivity). However, for atmosphere
L132@P2: retrieval the broad ~8-13 m region is typically used, as its
L133@P2: water vapor features are needed to characterize the water
L134@P2: column density and lower atmospheric temperature.
L135@P2: 2.2. Atmosphere and Emissivity Retrieval
L136@P2: The above 
L137@P2:  minimization approach is used to retrieve
L138@P2: atmospheric parameters in addition to surface temperatures.
L139@P2: We assume that the scene dimensions are small enough that
L140@P2: a single, homogenous atmosphere suffices. The model
L141@P2: calculations of (), L() and L() depend on assumed
L142@P2: atmospheric species and temperature profiles. In the 8-13
L143@P2: m region the most prominent atmospheric species is water
L144@P2: vapor, and under clear conditions the key variables are the
L145@P2: column water vapor and the air temperature near the ground.
L146@P2: The challenge is to specify a family of plausible and
L147@P2: diverse trial atmospheres using a small number of variables.
L148@P2: FLAASH-IR specifies a three-dimensional grid of
L149@P2: parameters controlling surface air temperature, water vapor
L150@P2: column density or humidity, and ozone concentration. The
L151@P2: parameters, typically a temperature shift and concentration
L152@P2: scalings, perturb the profiles of a user-selected
L153@P2: seasonal/latitude MODTRAN model atmosphere.
L154@P2: Tabulations of (), L() and L() spectra are derived
L155@P2: from the MODTRAN5 outputs, and polynomial fitting is
L156@P2: used to interpolate the spectra between these grid points.
L157@P2: Partial cloud cover is modeled by blending the clear sky

L161@P2: The best-fit atmosphere model is retrieved from of order
L162@P2: ten selected pixel spectra by minimizing the total 

L164@P2: respect to both T and the atmospheric parameters. The
L165@P2: spectra are selected to be diverse in shape and brightness, so
L166@P2: that different surface temperatures and emissivities are
L167@P2: represented. Low emissivity (reflective) materials provide
L168@P2: valuable information on L(). The 
L169@P2:  minimization
L170@P2: involves a one-dimensional surface temperature search on
L171@P2: the selected pixels embedded within a three-dimensional
L172@P2: atmosphere search, which is conducted using a downhill
L173@P2: simplex method. Finally, the retrieved atmosphere is used in
L174@P2: a one-dimensional search to derive surface temperature and
L175@P2: emissivity or reflectance for each pixel in the image. The
L176@P2: emissivity can be refined with a spectral “polishing” option
L177@P2: [8], in which smoothed emissivity spectra retrieved from the
L178@P2: selected pixels are input to a least squares procedure that
L179@P2: recalculates some or all of the atmospheric components,
L180@P2: (), L() and L(), which are then used in subsequent
L181@P2: retrievals.
L182@P2: 3. EXPERIMENT
L183@P2: The Telops Inc. Hyper-Cam LW is a portable imaging
L184@P2: Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer operating in
L185@P2: the 8-12 μm range. The detector is a 320x256 PV-MCT
L186@P2: focal plane array detector that can be windowed and
L187@P2: formatted to fit the desired image size and decrease the
L188@P2: acquisition time. The pixel IFOV is 0.35 mrad, and spectral
L189@P2: resolution is user selectable from 0.25 to 150 cm-1. The
L190@P2: Hyper-Cam LW has recently been integrated into an aircraft
L191@P2: for nadir-viewing measurements. The aircraft platform
L192@P2: includes a motion-compensating mirror that stabilizes the
L193@P2: images over acquisition times of typically ~1 s. Overlapping
L194@P2-3: images can be acquired and assembled into georectified mosaics. A visible camera is bore-sighted with the HyperCam. The data analyzed here, at 6 cm-1 resolution, were
L195@P3: taken of the Jean Gaulin refinery in Saint-Romuald, QC,
L196@P3: Canada at 11:30 AM on May 6, 2013 from an altitude of
L197@P3: 1.55 km. A 294x294-pixel sub-image of the mosaic is shown
L198@P3: in Fig. 1a. The corresponding visible image is in Fig. 1b.
L199@P3: 4. RESULTS
L200@P3: The refinery image was processed with FLAASH-IR using a
L201@P3: base MODTRAN Subarctic Summer model atmosphere and
L202@P3: a spectral polishing option. The diverse spectra for the
L203@P3: atmosphere retrieval were taken as averages of pixel spectral
L204@P3: clusters centered on automatically extracted endmembers.
L205@P3: As surfaces become highly reflective, surface temperature
L206@P3: becomes indeterminate; a lower bound of 7 C was assumed.
L207@P3: The output image is in reflectance versus wavelength. The
L208@P3: retrieved atmosphere has 1300 atm-cm of water vapor and a
L209@P3: surface air temperature of 27 C. The latter is close to the
L210@P3: recorded temperature of 25 C at the nearby Jean Lesage
L211@P3: Airport.
L212@P3: Fig. 1c shows the retrieved sub-image reflectance in
L213@P3: false color. Metal roofs, equipment coverings and pipes
L214@P3: appear in bright contrast against the other materials. Fig. 1d
L215@P3: shows the FLAASH-IR fit error, . Large errors, typically
L216@P3: up to ~50 µflicks, appear at object edges. These large errors
L217@P3: are caused by slight misregistrations of the frames in the
L218@P3: interferogram, resulting in some spectral corruption.
L219@P3: However, away from the edges the fit errors are much closer
L220@P3: to those observed in static Hyper-Cam measurements [8], as
L221@P3: low as ~6 µflicks in shadows, but several times larger than
L222@P3: this with reflective surfaces. Fig. 1e shows the retrieved
L223@P3: surface temperature map. The coolest shadows are around
L224@P3: 17 C; the sunlit areas are up to ~50 C except for a few “hot
L225@P3: spots”, which may include sensor anomalies. The most
L226@P3: reflective materials are pinned to the lower limit of 7 C.
L227@P3: Figs. 2a and b show example radiance and reflectance
L228@P3: spectra of various materials in the image. Consistent with
L229@P3: Fig. 1d, the reflectance “noise” is lowest for blackbodies
L230@P3: near ambient temperature. The metallic radiance spectra are
L231@P3: highly structured due to reflected downwelling illumination
L232@P3: from the 9.6 μm ozone band and 8-9 μm water vapor lines;
L233@P3: some residuals of these features appear in the reflectance
L234@P3: spectra. Dirt areas, appearing in red, have quartz-like
L235@P3: spectra typical of sandy soil. A green object in the radiance
L236@P3: image has a V-shaped spectrum that we interpret as plate
L237@P3: glass. Another spectrally distinct material is unknown.

L252@P4: 5. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
L253@P4: Processing LWIR hyperspectral imagery to reflectance or
L254@P4: emissivity via atmospheric compensation and TES affords
L255@P4: the opportunity to classify and identify solid materials with
L256@P4: minimal interference from the atmosphere. This is the first
L257@P4: such study of data from an aircraft-mounted Hyper-Cam
L258@P4: FTIR sensor. Acquiring FTIR imagery from a moving
L259@P4: platform is extremely challenging due to the potential for
L260@P4: both spatial misregistration and vibration effects on the
L261@P4: optics. Not surprisingly, the reflectance results are noisier
L262@P4: than what we have obtained from a stationary Hyper-Cam
L263@P4: [8] as well as from some other sensors. The noise level
L264@P4: might well be reduced with improvements in the hardware
L265@P4: and software, but even with the present limitations the
L266@P4: spectra and temperature maps should have considerable
L267@P4: utility for remote object and material identification.
